subject: chemistry

items.q:
Ammonia reacts with water:
NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
Which species acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid in the forward reaction?
items.correct: H₂O, as it donates a proton to NH₃
items.misconception: NH₃, as it gains a proton to form NH₄⁺
items.why: The two definitions are learned as a pair of near-identical phrases and are easily swapped. Students also link 'acid' with 'gaining H' because acids contain H, so the species that ends up with more hydrogen seems the acidic one. Follow the H⁺: the species that loses H⁺ is the acid, the species that gains H⁺ is the base. In NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻, H₂O loses H⁺ (acid) and NH₃ gains it (base).
items.specStatementText: Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton donor and a Brønsted–Lowry base is a proton acceptor.
items.random_wrong: OH⁻, as it forms when H₂O loses a proton

items.q: Copper(II) oxide, CuO, is insoluble in water. It reacts with dilute sulfuric acid to form copper(II) sulfate and water. How should copper(II) oxide be classified?
items.correct: As a base, but it is not an alkali
items.misconception: As an alkali, as it neutralizes an acid
items.why: Pre-16 courses often use the words interchangeably and meet mostly soluble bases (NaOH, KOH, ammonia solution), and everyday language uses 'alkaline' for anything basic. All alkalis are bases, but a base need only accept protons. Copper(II) oxide accepts H⁺ from an acid (CuO + 2H⁺ → Cu²⁺ + H₂O), so it is a base, but it is insoluble in water, so it is not an alkali.
items.specStatementText: Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton donor and a Brønsted–Lowry base is a proton acceptor.
items.random_wrong: As neither, as it contains no OH⁻ ions

items.q: Which pair of species is a conjugate acid–base pair?
items.correct: H₂PO₄⁻ and HPO₄²⁻
items.misconception: H₃PO₄ and HPO₄²⁻
items.why: Species such as H₃PO₄, H₂PO₄⁻, HPO₄²⁻ and PO₄³⁻ are listed together as 'the phosphate family', so students treat any two of them as partners. The definition requires a difference of a single proton. Remove one H and lower the charge by one unit to get the conjugate base: H₃PO₄ → H₂PO₄⁻ → HPO₄²⁻ → PO₄³⁻; only neighbours in this sequence are conjugate pairs.
items.specStatementText: A pair of species differing by a single proton is called a conjugate acid–base pair.
items.random_wrong: CH₃COOH and NH₃

items.q:
Dihydrogenphosphate ions react with ammonia:
H₂PO₄⁻(aq) + NH₃(aq) ⇌ HPO₄²⁻(aq) + NH₄⁺(aq)
Which statement describes the role of H₂PO₄⁻ in the forward reaction?
items.correct: It is an acid, as it gives up a proton to NH₃
items.misconception: It is a base, since negative ions only accept H⁺
items.why: Many familiar bases are anions (OH⁻, CO₃²⁻, CH₃COO⁻), and the attraction between a negative ion and H⁺ is easy to picture, so charge is taken as the deciding feature. Decide from the reaction. In H₂PO₄⁻ + NH₃ ⇌ HPO₄²⁻ + NH₄⁺ the anion H₂PO₄⁻ loses H⁺, so here it is an acid.
items.specStatementText: Some species can act as both Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases.
items.random_wrong: It is a base, as it loses a proton to NH₃

items.q: 10.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid is diluted with distilled water to a total volume of 1.00 dm³. What is the pH of the diluted solution?
items.why:
Students think of pH as a property of the substance ('hydrochloric acid has pH 1') rather than of a particular solution, and dilution calculations are often done in a separate topic from pH. pH depends on [H⁺], which depends on how much water is present. Diluting 10.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl to 1.00 dm³ lowers [H⁺] 100-fold, to 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, so the pH rises by 2 units to 3.00.

Working: n(HCl) = 0.100 mol dm⁻³ × (10.0/1000) dm³ = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol. [H⁺] = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 1.00 dm³ = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ (HCl is fully ionized). pH = −log₁₀(1.00 × 10⁻³) = 3.00.
items.specStatementText: The pH scale can be used to describe the [H⁺] of a solution: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]; [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ
items.working: n(HCl) = 0.100 mol dm⁻³ × (10.0/1000) dm³ = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol. [H⁺] = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 1.00 dm³ = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ (HCl is fully ionized). pH = −log₁₀(1.00 × 10⁻³) = 3.00.

items.q: Which statement about measuring the pH of an aqueous solution is correct?
items.correct: A calibrated pH meter can give the pH to about 0.01 unit.
items.misconception: Universal indicator is as precise as a pH meter.
items.why: Colour charts print a single pH number beside each colour, which suggests a one-to-one match between colour and an exact value. Each colour on the chart covers a range of pH, and judging a colour is subjective. A pH meter gives a numerical reading, typically to 0.01 unit, once it has been calibrated.
items.specStatementText: The pH scale can be used to describe the [H⁺] of a solution: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]; [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ
items.random_wrong: A new pH meter reads accurately before it is calibrated.

items.q: At 298 K, solution P has [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ and solution Q has [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. Kw = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 298 K. How does [OH⁻] in P compare with [OH⁻] in Q?
items.correct: It is 100 times smaller in P than in Q.
items.misconception: It is 100 times larger in P than in Q.
items.why:
The equation H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻ produces the two ions in a 1 : 1 ratio, and students carry that ratio over to solutions to which an acid or a base has been added. The 1 : 1 ratio applies only to ions produced by water itself. Adding a base supplies extra OH⁻, and the water equilibrium shifts left, lowering [H⁺] so that [H⁺][OH⁻] stays equal to Kw.

Working: [OH⁻] = Kw/[H⁺]. P: 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ / (1.0 × 10⁻³) = 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ mol dm⁻³. Q: 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ / (1.0 × 10⁻⁵) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ mol dm⁻³. Ratio P : Q = 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ / 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ = 1/100.
items.specStatementText: The ion product constant of water, Kw, shows an inverse relationship between [H⁺] and [OH⁻]. Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻]
items.random_wrong: It is the same, as acid has no effect on [OH⁻].

items.q: A student's data show that an aqueous solution at 323 K has [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 2.34 × 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³, so its pH is 6.63. Which statement about this solution is correct?
items.correct: It is neutral, as its [H⁺] and [OH⁻] are equal.
items.misconception: It is acidic, as its pH is lower than 7.00.
items.why: pH 7 is taught as 'the neutral point' with the temperature (298 K) rarely stated, and colour charts mark 7 as neutral. The defining test is the relative size of [H⁺] and [OH⁻]. The value pH 7.00 follows from Kw = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 298 K; if a solution at another temperature has [H⁺] = [OH⁻], it is neutral whatever its pH.
items.specStatementText: The ion product constant of water, Kw, shows an inverse relationship between [H⁺] and [OH⁻]. Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻]
items.random_wrong: It is acidic, as it contains H⁺(aq) ions.

items.q: A solution of nitric acid, HNO₃(aq), has a concentration of 0.0010 mol dm⁻³. Which statement about this solution is correct?
items.correct: It is a dilute solution of an acid that is fully ionized.
items.misconception: It is a weak acid, as its concentration is low.
items.why: In everyday language 'strong' and 'weak' describe concentration (strong coffee, weak squash), and the most familiar strong acids and bases are handled as concentrated reagents with extreme pH values. Strength is a property of the acid or base; concentration is a property of the solution. 0.0010 mol dm⁻³ HNO₃ is dilute but still strong (fully ionized); 10 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH is concentrated but still weak. Likewise 0.10 mol dm⁻³ NaOH has pH 13.0 whereas 0.10 mol dm⁻³ NH₃ has pH 11.1: at equal concentration the weak base gives the lower pH.
items.specStatementText: Strong and weak acids and bases differ in the extent of ionization.
items.random_wrong: It contains mainly HNO₃ molecules with a few ions.

items.q:
Hydrogen chloride reacts with water:
HCl(aq) + H₂O(l) → H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)
The position of this equilibrium lies so far to the right that the reaction is effectively complete. Which statement about this reaction is correct?
items.correct: Cl⁻ is a weaker base than H₂O.
items.misconception: Cl⁻ is the acid, since HCl forms it.
items.why: Every Brønsted–Lowry equation contains two acids and two bases (one of each on each side), and students are asked to label all four, so the reactant and its conjugate are easily swapped. Label the reactants first: in the forward reaction the reactant that loses H⁺ is the acid and the one that gains H⁺ is the base. Their products are, respectively, the conjugate base and the conjugate acid.
items.specStatementText: Strong and weak acids and bases differ in the extent of ionization.
items.random_wrong: H₃O⁺ is a stronger acid than HCl.

items.q: Separate 25.0 cm³ samples of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) and 0.100 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH(aq) are each titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq). Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Both need the same volume of NaOH(aq), as the acid amounts are equal.
items.misconception: The HCl needs more NaOH(aq), as it releases more H⁺ ions in water.
items.why: Students correctly learn that a weak acid solution contains fewer H⁺ ions at any moment and assume only those ions can react with the base. The amount of base needed depends on the amount of acid, not on its strength. When OH⁻ removes H⁺, the equilibrium HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻ shifts to the right, so eventually every HA molecule has donated its proton.
items.specStatementText: Strong and weak acids and bases differ in the extent of ionization.
items.random_wrong: Both acids start at the same pH, as their acid concentrations are equal.

items.q: Aqueous ethanoic acid is added to solid sodium carbonate until the reaction stops. What are the products of the reaction?
items.correct: sodium ethanoate, water and carbon dioxide
items.misconception: sodium ethanoate and water, with no gas
items.why: 'Acid + base → salt + water' is the first general equation students learn, and the metal oxide and hydroxide examples all fit it. Write the equation from the proton transfer. CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂, so carbonates also give CO₂. NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺ and CH₃NH₂ + H⁺ → CH₃NH₃⁺: the base simply gains a proton, so no water forms.
items.specStatementText: Acids react with bases in neutralization reactions.
items.random_wrong: sodium ethanoate, hydrogen and carbon dioxide

items.q: Methylammonium chloride, CH₃NH₃Cl, is a salt. Which statement about this salt is correct?
items.correct: It forms from HCl and CH₃NH₂, with no water produced.
items.misconception: Its parent base is CH₃NH₃OH, since a base must contain OH.
items.why: The Arrhenius picture from earlier courses (bases produce OH⁻) and the familiar examples NaOH and KOH make 'OH' look like the defining feature of a base; the OH group in alcohols looks the same on paper; bottles of ammonia solution labelled 'ammonium hydroxide, NH₄OH' reinforce the idea. Classify by behaviour, not by the letters in the formula. A base accepts H⁺ using a lone pair: ammonia and amines do this through the lone pair on nitrogen. The O–H group of an alcohol is covalently bonded and is not released as OH⁻.
items.specStatementText: Acids react with bases in neutralization reactions.
items.random_wrong: It forms from HCl and CH₃NH₂, with water as a second product.

items.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) is placed in a flask and 25.0 cm³ of distilled water is added. The mixture is then titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq). At what pH does the pH curve intercept the pH axis (0.00 cm³ of NaOH(aq) added)?
items.why:
Both keys are labelled 'log' in speech, both give a 'logarithm', and students meet ln in other contexts (and later in the Arrhenius equation). pH is defined with log₁₀. ln x = 2.303 log₁₀x, so using ln gives an answer 2.303 times too large: for [H⁺] = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, −ln gives 6.91 instead of 3.00.

Working: n(HCl) = 0.100 mol dm⁻³ × 0.0250 dm³ = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol. Volume in flask = 25.0 + 25.0 = 50.0 cm³ = 0.0500 dm³. [H⁺] = 2.50 × 10⁻³ / 0.0500 = 0.0500 mol dm⁻³. pH = −log₁₀(0.0500) = 1.30.
items.specStatementText: pH curves for neutralization reactions involving strong acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.

items.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) at 298 K until 50.0 cm³ of NaOH(aq) has been added. Which statement about the pH curve is correct?
items.correct: At 25.0 cm³ the pH is 7, as only NaCl(aq) and water are present.
items.misconception: After 25.0 cm³ the pH stays at 7, as all the acid is neutralized.
items.why: Neutralization is described as producing a 'neutral' solution, so students treat pH 7 as the end state of the reaction rather than as one point on the curve. Neutralization is complete at the equivalence point, but further NaOH added has nothing to react with, so OH⁻ accumulates. For 0.100 mol dm⁻³ reagents the pH is about 12.5 after twice the equivalence volume has been added.
items.specStatementText: pH curves for neutralization reactions involving strong acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.
items.random_wrong: The pH rises by an equal amount for each 1.00 cm³ of NaOH(aq) added.

items.q: An aqueous solution at 298 K has [H⁺] = 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³. What is the pOH of the solution?
items.why:
The quantities have the same form (−log₁₀ of something) and the same size range, and many problems involve converting between them, so students lose track of which one a given number is. Label every value with what it refers to. A pOH of 4.30 means [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁴·³⁰; the pH is 14.00 − 4.30 = 9.70. At the half-equivalence point of a weak base, pOH = pKb, so pKb = 14.00 − pH.

Working: pH = −log₁₀(5.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 5.30. pOH = 14.00 − pH = 14.00 − 5.30 = 8.70 (at 298 K). Check: [OH⁻] = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ mol dm⁻³; −log₁₀(2.0 × 10⁻⁹) = 8.70.
items.specStatementText: The pOH scale describes the [OH⁻] of a solution. pOH = −log₁₀[OH⁻]; [OH⁻] = 10⁻ᵖᴼᴴ

items.q: At 298 K the pKa of methanoic acid, HCOOH, is 3.75 and the pKa of ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, is 4.76. Which statement about 0.10 mol dm⁻³ solutions of the two acids is correct?
items.correct: Methanoic acid is ionized to a greater extent than ethanoic acid.
items.misconception: Ethanoic acid is the stronger acid, as its pKa is the larger.
items.why: Students read larger numbers as 'more' of a property, and the minus sign in the definition inverts the relationship without being noticed. With Ka values, a larger Ka does mean stronger, which reinforces 'bigger = stronger'. Because of the minus sign, each unit decrease in pKa is a tenfold increase in Ka. Methanoic acid (pKa 3.75) is about ten times stronger than ethanoic acid (pKa 4.76). The same holds for bases: the smaller the pKb, the stronger the base.
items.specStatementText: The strengths of weak acids and bases are described by their Ka, Kb, pKa or pKb values.
items.random_wrong: Both are ionized to the same extent, as both are weak acids.

items.q: At 298 K the pKa of the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, is 9.25 and the pKa of the methylammonium ion, CH₃NH₃⁺, is 10.66. Which statement about the bases NH₃ and CH₃NH₂ is correct?
items.correct: CH₃NH₂ is the stronger base, since its pKb is 3.34.
items.misconception: CH₃NH₂ is the stronger base, and its pKb is 1.31.
items.why:
Students carry the form of the concentration equation (a product) over to the logarithmic equation without applying the rule log(ab) = log a + log b. −log₁₀([H⁺][OH⁻]) = −log₁₀[H⁺] + (−log₁₀[OH⁻]), so pH + pOH = pKw = 14.00 at 298 K. For [H⁺] = 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³, pH = 5.30 and pOH = 14.00 − 5.30 = 8.70, not 14.00/5.30.

Working: pKb = 14.00 − pKa(conjugate acid). NH₃: 14.00 − 9.25 = 4.75. CH₃NH₂: 14.00 − 10.66 = 3.34. Smaller pKb, larger Kb (10⁻³·³⁴ = 4.6 × 10⁻⁴ against 10⁻⁴·⁷⁵ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵), so CH₃NH₂ is the stronger base.
items.specStatementText: For a conjugate acid–base pair, the relationship Ka × Kb = Kw can be derived from the expressions for Ka and Kb.
items.random_wrong: NH₃ is the stronger base, since its pKb is 9.25.
items.working: pKb = 14.00 − pKa(conjugate acid). NH₃: 14.00 − 9.25 = 4.75. CH₃NH₂: 14.00 − 10.66 = 3.34. Smaller pKb, larger Kb (10⁻³·³⁴ = 4.6 × 10⁻⁴ against 10⁻⁴·⁷⁵ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵), so CH₃NH₂ is the stronger base.

items.q: What is the pH of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH(aq), at 298 K? Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵. Assume that the equilibrium concentration of CH₃COOH equals its initial concentration.
items.why:
Most pH calculations first met are for strong acids, where [H⁺] = [acid], and the shortcut is then applied to every acid. Only complete ionization makes [H⁺] = [acid]. 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl has pH 1.00, but 0.100 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH has pH about 2.9 because only about 1% of its molecules are ionized.

Working: CH₃COOH ⇌ H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻; [H⁺] = [CH₃COO⁻]; Ka ≈ [H⁺]²/0.100. [H⁺] = √(1.74 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.100) = √(1.74 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.32 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³. pH = −log₁₀(1.32 × 10⁻³) = 2.88.
items.specStatementText: For a conjugate acid–base pair, the relationship Ka × Kb = Kw can be derived from the expressions for Ka and Kb.

items.q: Aqueous solutions of sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃, and sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO₃, each of concentration 0.10 mol dm⁻³, are prepared at 298 K. pKa(H₂CO₃) = 6.35 and pKa(HCO₃⁻) = 10.33. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Na₂CO₃(aq) has the higher pH, as CO₃²⁻ has the smaller pKb (3.67).
items.misconception: NaHCO₃(aq) has the higher pH, since HCO₃⁻ has the larger pKa (10.33).
items.why:
Both members of a conjugate pair appear in the same equilibrium and data tables often give only one value per pair, so students assume that one number describes both species. Multiplying Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA] by Kb = [HA][OH⁻]/[A⁻] gives [H⁺][OH⁻] = Kw. So Kb = Kw/Ka: NH₄⁺ has pKa 9.25, so NH₃ has pKb 14.00 − 9.25 = 4.75.

Working: pKb(CO₃²⁻) = 14.00 − pKa(HCO₃⁻) = 14.00 − 10.33 = 3.67. pKb(HCO₃⁻) = 14.00 − pKa(H₂CO₃) = 14.00 − 6.35 = 7.65. Smaller pKb, stronger base, higher [OH⁻], higher pH for Na₂CO₃(aq).
items.specStatementText: The pH of a salt solution depends on the relative strengths of the parent acid and base.
items.random_wrong: NaHCO₃(aq) is acidic, as HCO₃⁻ contains an H⁺ that it can donate.
items.working: pKb(CO₃²⁻) = 14.00 − pKa(HCO₃⁻) = 14.00 − 10.33 = 3.67. pKb(HCO₃⁻) = 14.00 − pKa(H₂CO₃) = 14.00 − 6.35 = 7.65. Smaller pKb, stronger base, higher [OH⁻], higher pH for Na₂CO₃(aq).

items.q: Which equation represents the hydrolysis reaction that determines the pH of aqueous ammonium chloride, NH₄Cl(aq)?
items.correct: NH₄⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₃(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq)
items.misconception: Cl⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HCl(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
items.why: Students expect 'strong' to be shared within a pair, and they see Cl⁻ as a negative ion that should attract H⁺ strongly. HCl is strong because Cl⁻ holds on to H⁺ so weakly that the proton passes almost completely to water. A weak hold on H⁺ is what 'weak base' means, so a strong acid has a very weak conjugate base.
items.specStatementText: The pH of a salt solution depends on the relative strengths of the parent acid and base.
items.random_wrong: NH₄Cl(s) + aq → NH₄⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)

items.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid (pKa = 4.76) is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) at 298 K. What is the pH after 12.5 cm³ of NaOH(aq) has been added?
items.why:
Both terms contain 'equivalence', both are marked on the same curve, and the half-equivalence point is often introduced only as 'where pH = pKa' without a volume. Find the equivalence volume first, then halve it. For 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH, equivalence is at 25.0 cm³ (pH about 8.7) and half-equivalence at 12.5 cm³ (pH 4.76).

Working: n(CH₃COOH) = 0.100 × 0.0250 = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol; equivalence at 25.0 cm³ NaOH. After 12.5 cm³: n(NaOH) = 1.25 × 10⁻³ mol, leaving 1.25 × 10⁻³ mol CH₃COOH and forming 1.25 × 10⁻³ mol CH₃COO⁻. [CH₃COOH] = [CH₃COO⁻], so [H⁺] = Ka and pH = pKa = 4.76.
items.specStatementText: pH curves of different combinations of strong and weak monoprotic acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.
items.working: n(CH₃COOH) = 0.100 × 0.0250 = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol; equivalence at 25.0 cm³ NaOH. After 12.5 cm³: n(NaOH) = 1.25 × 10⁻³ mol, leaving 1.25 × 10⁻³ mol CH₃COOH and forming 1.25 × 10⁻³ mol CH₃COO⁻. [CH₃COOH] = [CH₃COO⁻], so [H⁺] = Ka and pH = pKa = 4.76.

items.q: 25.0 cm³ of a 0.100 mol dm⁻³ aqueous solution of a base, B, is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) at 298 K. The pH curve starts at pH 11.1 and falls gently through a region in which the pH is 9.25 at 12.5 cm³. It then falls steeply near 25.0 cm³, through an equivalence point at pH 5.3, and levels off near pH 1.5 by 50.0 cm³. Which statement about B is correct?
items.correct: B is a weak base, and the pKa of its conjugate acid is 9.25.
items.misconception: B is a strong base, as the curve has a steep section.
items.why: The strong acid–strong base curve, with its long vertical section, is learned first, so steepness becomes associated with strength of both reactants. The steep section arises because the titrant (here a strong acid) changes the pH sharply once the analyte is used up. Evidence that the analyte is weak includes an intercept closer to 7 than a strong base of that concentration would give, and a gently sloping buffer region.
items.specStatementText: pH curves of different combinations of strong and weak monoprotic acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.
items.random_wrong: B is a weak base, and the pKb of B itself is 9.25.

items.q:
An indicator, HInd, has pKa = 3.7:
HInd(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + Ind⁻(aq)
HInd is red and Ind⁻ is yellow. What colour does the indicator show in a solution of pH 6.0, and why?
items.correct: Yellow, as Ind⁻ predominates when the pH is above the pKa.
items.misconception: Red, as the solution is acidic, with its pH below 7.
items.why: Litmus, the first indicator most students meet, changes near pH 7, and indicators are introduced as showing 'acid or alkali', which seems to make 7 the natural switching point. An indicator is a weak acid, HInd ⇌ H⁺ + Ind⁻, and switches when [H⁺] ≈ Ka, i.e. at pH ≈ pKa. An indicator with pKa 3.7 already shows the colour of Ind⁻ at pH 5, although that solution is acidic.
items.specStatementText: Acid–base indicators are weak acids, where the components of the conjugate acid–base pair have different colours. The pH of the end point of an indicator, where it changes colour, approximately corresponds to its pKa value.
items.random_wrong: Red, as HInd predominates when the pH is above the pKa.

items.q: Universal indicator shows a different colour at almost every whole-number pH from about 1 to 14. What is the reason for this?
items.correct: It is a mixture of indicators whose colour changes occur at different pH values.
items.misconception: It is a single weak acid whose one equilibrium shifts gradually across that range.
items.why: Universal indicator is bought as one bottle with one name, and its colour chart looks like a smooth spectrum from one substance. One indicator has only two coloured forms and changes over about 2 pH units (pKa ± 1). A wide range of colours requires several indicators with different pKa values, each changing colour in its own part of the range.
items.specStatementText: Acid–base indicators are weak acids, where the components of the conjugate acid–base pair have different colours. The pH of the end point of an indicator, where it changes colour, approximately corresponds to its pKa value.
items.random_wrong: It reacts with the acid or alkali present, forming a differently coloured salt.

items.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid (pKa = 4.76) is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) at 298 K. Three indicators are available, with these pH ranges: methyl orange 3.1–4.4; bromothymol blue 6.0–7.6; phenolphthalein 8.3–10.0. Which choice of indicator, with its reason, is correct?
items.correct: Phenolphthalein, as the salt CH₃COONa makes the equivalence pH above 7.
items.misconception: Methyl orange, as its range is close to the pKa of ethanoic acid.
items.why: The phrase 'end point ≈ pKa' is remembered without noting whose pKa it is, and the analyte's pKa is the one number given in the problem. The end point is where the indicator's HInd and Ind⁻ are equal, at pH ≈ pKa(indicator). For ethanoic acid (pKa 4.76) titrated with NaOH, pH 4.76 is in the buffer region, far from the equivalence point (about 8.7), so an indicator changing near 4.76 would give an end point far too early.
items.specStatementText: An appropriate indicator for a titration has an end point range that coincides with the pH at the equivalence point.
items.random_wrong: Bromothymol blue, as the equivalence point of a titration is at pH 7.

items.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the end point of a titration from its equivalence point?
items.correct: The end point is where the indicator changes colour; the equivalence point is where acid and base have reacted in the stoichiometric ratio.
items.misconception: The end point and the equivalence point are the same point by definition, so the two terms can be used interchangeably in any titration.
items.why: In school titrations the end point is used as the equivalence point, and the two terms are often used interchangeably in instructions. One is defined by stoichiometry, the other by an observation. With the wrong indicator, the end point can be several cm³ away from the equivalence point.
items.specStatementText: An appropriate indicator for a titration has an end point range that coincides with the pH at the equivalence point.
items.random_wrong: The equivalence point is the point where the pH equals 7; the end point is the pH at which the colour of the chosen indicator changes.

items.q: Which mixture, made up to 1.00 dm³ with water, is a buffer solution?
items.correct: NH₃ (0.30 mol) with HCl (0.15 mol)
items.misconception: CH₃COOH (0.30 mol) with NaOH (0.30 mol)
items.why: Students learn that a buffer can be made by adding a strong base to a weak acid and do not work through the stoichiometry of the reaction. Work out what is left after reaction: 0.20 mol CH₃COOH + 0.10 mol NaOH leaves 0.10 mol CH₃COOH and 0.10 mol CH₃COO⁻ (a buffer). 0.10 mol of each leaves only 0.10 mol CH₃COO⁻, which is not a buffer.
items.specStatementText: A buffer solution is one that resists change in pH on the addition of small amounts of acid or alkali.
items.random_wrong: HCl (0.15 mol) with NaCl (0.30 mol)

items.q: A buffer solution contains 0.10 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH(aq) and 0.10 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COONa(aq). A small amount of HCl(aq) is added. Which statement about the buffer's response is correct?
items.correct: CH₃COO⁻ ions react with the added H⁺, forming CH₃COOH.
items.misconception: CH₃COOH molecules react with the added H⁺, removing it.
items.why: Students match 'acidic buffer' or 'the acid in the buffer' with 'handles acid' without asking which component can actually react with the added ion. Only a base can remove H⁺ and only an acid can remove OH⁻. In CH₃COOH/CH₃COO⁻, CH₃COO⁻ takes up added H⁺; in NH₃/NH₄⁺, NH₄⁺ takes up added OH⁻.
items.specStatementText: A buffer solution is one that resists change in pH on the addition of small amounts of acid or alkali.
items.random_wrong: Na⁺ ions combine with the added Cl⁻, forming NaCl.

items.q: A buffer solution at 298 K contains 0.20 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH and 0.10 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COONa. Ka(CH₃COOH) = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵. What is the pH of the buffer?
items.why:
The expression is often remembered as pH = pKa + log₁₀([A⁻]/[HA]), with the salt on top, and this ratio is then carried into the [H⁺] expression without inverting it. Rearrange Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA] to [H⁺] = Ka[HA]/[A⁻]. A sense check: a buffer with more acid than salt must be more acidic than pKa.

Working: Ka = [H⁺][CH₃COO⁻]/[CH₃COOH], so [H⁺] = Ka × [CH₃COOH]/[CH₃COO⁻] = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ × (0.20/0.10) = 3.48 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. pH = −log₁₀(3.48 × 10⁻⁵) = 4.46.
items.specStatementText: The pH of a buffer solution depends on both: the pKa or pKb of its acid or base; the ratio of the concentration of acid or base to the concentration of the conjugate base or acid.
items.working: Ka = [H⁺][CH₃COO⁻]/[CH₃COOH], so [H⁺] = Ka × [CH₃COOH]/[CH₃COO⁻] = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ × (0.20/0.10) = 3.48 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. pH = −log₁₀(3.48 × 10⁻⁵) = 4.46.

items.q: A buffer containing 0.20 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH and 0.10 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COO⁻ has pH 4.46. It is diluted with an equal volume of water. To a first approximation, what happens to its pH?
items.correct: It stays at about 4.46, as the ratio [CH₃COOH]/[CH₃COO⁻] is unchanged.
items.misconception: It rises by about 0.30, as [H⁺] halves when the volume doubles.
items.why: Students correctly learn that diluting a strong acid lowers [H⁺] in proportion and apply the same rule to buffers. In a buffer, [H⁺] is set by Ka and the ratio [HA]/[A⁻], not by the total concentration. Dilution leaves the ratio unchanged, so to a first approximation the pH does not change; it does reduce the buffer's capacity.
items.specStatementText: The pH of a buffer solution depends on both: the pKa or pKb of its acid or base; the ratio of the concentration of acid or base to the concentration of the conjugate base or acid.
items.random_wrong: It rises to pH 7, as the added water neutralizes the acid present.

items.q: Solid magnesium oxide, MgO, is added to dilute nitric acid, HNO₃(aq). Which statement about what happens is correct?
items.correct: MgO and HNO₃ react in a 1 : 2 mole ratio, as O²⁻ accepts two H⁺.
items.misconception: MgO and HNO₃ react in a 1 : 1 mole ratio, as NaOH and HCl do too.
items.why:
The first neutralization students meet and practise, NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O, is 1 : 1, and that ratio is carried over to other reactions without balancing the equation (the 'ignoring the mole ratio' error). Write the formula of the salt from its ions (Mg²⁺ and NO₃⁻ give Mg(NO₃)₂), then balance the equation: the amount of H⁺ donated by the acid must equal the amount of H⁺ accepted by the base.

Working: MgO(s) + 2HNO₃(aq) → Mg(NO₃)₂(aq) + H₂O(l). Atoms: Mg 1 = 1; N 2 = 2; O 1 + 6 = 6 + 1; H 2 = 2. O²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O, so n(HNO₃) : n(MgO) = 2 : 1.
items.specStatementText: Acids react with bases in neutralization reactions.
items.random_wrong: No reaction occurs, as MgO is not a base: it has no hydroxide ions.
items.working: MgO(s) + 2HNO₃(aq) → Mg(NO₃)₂(aq) + H₂O(l). Atoms: Mg 1 = 1; N 2 = 2; O 1 + 6 = 6 + 1; H 2 = 2. O²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O, so n(HNO₃) : n(MgO) = 2 : 1.

items.q: Solid sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO₃, is added to dilute hydrochloric acid, HCl(aq). Which statement about the reaction is correct?
items.correct: NaHCO₃ and HCl react in a 1 : 1 mole ratio, as HCO₃⁻ accepts one H⁺.
items.misconception: NaHCO₃ and HCl react in a 1 : 2 mole ratio, as carbonates do.
items.why:
Carbonates and hydrogencarbonates are taught together with one word equation (acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide), so the balanced carbonate equation, with its 2 mol of acid, is reused for the hydrogencarbonate. Count the protons each ion accepts to form H₂O and CO₂: CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂, but HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂.

Working: NaHCO₃(s) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). Atoms: Na 1 = 1; H 1 + 1 = 2; C 1 = 1; O 3 = 1 + 2; Cl 1 = 1. HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂, so n(HCl) : n(NaHCO₃) = 1 : 1.
items.specStatementText: Acids react with bases in neutralization reactions.
items.random_wrong: Only NaCl and water form, as neutralization gives salt and water.
items.working: NaHCO₃(s) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). Atoms: Na 1 = 1; H 1 + 1 = 2; C 1 = 1; O 3 = 1 + 2; Cl 1 = 1. HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂, so n(HCl) : n(NaHCO₃) = 1 : 1.

items.q: Which equation represents the hydrolysis reaction that determines the pH of aqueous sodium ethanoate, CH₃COONa(aq)?
items.correct: CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COOH(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
items.misconception: CH₃COONa(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COOH(aq) + NaOH(aq)
items.why: The word 'hydrolysis' suggests splitting by water, and students picture the neutralization equation run backwards. Only the ion derived from the weak parent hydrolyses. HCl is strong, so it does not re-form as molecules in water; Cl⁻ is a spectator. The equation shows NH₄⁺ donating H⁺ to water.
items.specStatementText: The pH of a salt solution depends on the relative strengths of the parent acid and base.
items.random_wrong: CH₃COONa(s) + aq → CH₃COO⁻(aq) + Na⁺(aq)

items.q: Which mixture, made up to 1.00 dm³ with water, is an acidic buffer solution?
items.correct: CH₃COOH (0.20 mol) with KOH (0.10 mol)
items.misconception: HNO₃ (0.10 mol) with NaNO₃ (0.20 mol)
items.why: Buffers are introduced as 'an acid and its salt', and the condition that the acid must be weak is lost. Buffering requires a reservoir of both HA and A⁻ to react with added OH⁻ and H⁺. Cl⁻ is too weak a base to remove added H⁺, and HCl is fully ionized, so the mixture behaves as a strong acid solution.
items.specStatementText: A buffer solution is one that resists change in pH on the addition of small amounts of acid or alkali.
items.random_wrong: CH₃COOH (0.10 mol) with NaOH (0.20 mol)

items.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH(aq) (pKa = 4.76) is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NH₃(aq) (pKb = 4.75) at 298 K. Which statement describes the pH curve?
items.correct: It has no near-vertical section near 25.0 cm³, as acid and base are both weak.
items.misconception: It rises almost vertically near 25.0 cm³, from about pH 3 to about pH 11.
items.why: In strong acid–strong base titrations the vertical section spans pH 3 to 11 and almost any common indicator works, so students generalize. When a weak acid or weak base is involved the steep section is much shorter. For ethanoic acid with NaOH it runs from about pH 7 to 11, so methyl orange (3.1–4.4) changes colour well before equivalence.
items.specStatementText: pH curves of different combinations of strong and weak monoprotic acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.
items.random_wrong: It starts near pH 11, as that is the pH of the aqueous ammonia added.

items.q: Solution X is 0.0010 mol dm⁻³ KOH(aq). Solution Y is 2.0 mol dm⁻³ NH₃(aq). Which statement is correct?
items.correct: KOH is the stronger base, as it is fully ionized.
items.misconception: Both are strong bases, as both release OH⁻ ions in water.
items.why: The alkalis met first, NaOH and KOH, are strong, and 'alkali' and 'strong base' are introduced together; aqueous ammonia is also called an alkali, so it is grouped with them. Being an alkali is about dissolving and producing OH⁻(aq); being strong is about the extent of ionization. Decide strength from whether the reaction with water goes to completion.
items.specStatementText: Strong and weak acids and bases differ in the extent of ionization.
items.random_wrong: NH₃ is the stronger base, as solution Y is more concentrated.

items.q: 10.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid of pH 1.70 is diluted with distilled water to a total volume of 1.00 dm³ at 298 K. What is [H⁺] in the diluted solution?
items.correct: 0.00020 mol dm⁻³
items.misconception: 0.50 mol dm⁻³
items.why:
Inverting pH = −log₁₀[H⁺] takes two steps (change the sign, then take 10ˣ), and students press the 10ˣ key on the pH value itself; the size of the result is not checked. Rearrange first: log₁₀[H⁺] = −pH, so [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ. Check the answer: a solution with a pH above 0 has [H⁺] below 1 mol dm⁻³.

Working: [H⁺] in the original acid = 10⁻ᵖᴴ = 10⁻¹·⁷⁰ = 0.0200 mol dm⁻³. n(H⁺) = 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ × (10.0/1000) dm³ = 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol. [H⁺] after dilution = 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol ÷ 1.00 dm³ = 0.00020 mol dm⁻³ (2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³).
items.specStatementText: The pH scale can be used to describe the [H⁺] of a solution: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]; [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ
items.random_wrong: 0.020 mol dm⁻³

items.q: Which is a correct equation for HCO₃⁻ acting as a Brønsted–Lowry base in the forward reaction?
items.correct: HCO₃⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq) + H₂O(l)
items.misconception: HCO₃⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq) ⇌ H₂CO₃⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)
items.why: Students count atoms in formulae far more often than charges, and 'loses a hydrogen' is common shorthand for 'loses a proton'. A proton is H⁺, a hydrogen atom without its electron. The electron stays on the conjugate base, so its charge is one unit more negative than the acid's; a base that gains H⁺ becomes one unit more positive.
items.specStatementText: Some species can act as both Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases.
items.random_wrong: HCO₃⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq) ⇌ CO₃²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)

items.q: What is the formula of the conjugate base of ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH?
items.correct: CH₃COO⁻
items.misconception: CH₂COOH⁻
items.why: Acids are introduced as 'compounds containing hydrogen that release H⁺', so students count H atoms in formulae as a measure of acidity. Ionizability depends on bonding, not on the number of H atoms. CH₃COOH has four H atoms but is monoprotic and weak; HCl has one H atom and is strong.
items.specStatementText: A pair of species differing by a single proton is called a conjugate acid–base pair.
items.random_wrong: CH₃COO

items.q: Barium hydroxide, Ba(OH)₂, is a strong base that dissociates completely in water. What is the pH of 0.050 mol dm⁻³ Ba(OH)₂(aq) at 298 K?
items.why:
Nearly every worked example uses NaOH or KOH, in which one formula unit gives one OH⁻, so the 1 : 1 relationship is generalized without looking at the formula. Write the dissociation equation and read off the ratio: Ba(OH)₂(aq) → Ba²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq), so [OH⁻] = 2 × [Ba(OH)₂]. Then pOH = −log₁₀[OH⁻] and pH = 14.00 − pOH at 298 K.

Working: Ba(OH)₂(aq) → Ba²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq), so [OH⁻] = 2 × 0.050 = 0.10 mol dm⁻³. pOH = −log₁₀(0.10) = 1.00. At 298 K, pH + pOH = 14.00, so pH = 14.00 − 1.00 = 13.00.
items.specStatementText: The pOH scale describes the [OH⁻] of a solution. pOH = −log₁₀[OH⁻]; [OH⁻] = 10⁻ᵖᴼᴴ

items.q:
The table shows data at 298 K for four weak bases.
W: Kb = 4.4 × 10⁻⁴
X: pKb = 4.75
Y: Kb = 1.6 × 10⁻⁶
Z: pKb = 9.4
Which statement is correct?
items.correct: W is a stronger base than X, as Kb(W) is larger than Kb(X).
items.misconception: X and Y are equally strong, as both are weak bases.
items.why: At SL acids are sorted into two categories, strong and weak, and the category is sometimes treated as the whole description. 'Weak' only means 'partially ionized'. Ka values of weak acids span many orders of magnitude: methanoic acid (pKa 3.75) is stronger than ethanoic acid (pKa 4.76), which is much stronger than the ammonium ion (pKa 9.25).
items.specStatementText: The strengths of weak acids and bases are described by their Ka, Kb, pKa or pKb values.
items.random_wrong: Z is a stronger base than Y, as pKb(Z) is larger than pKb(Y).

items.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) is placed in a flask and 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) is added from a burette. The figure shows four sketched pH curves, A to D. Which curve shows how the pH in the flask changes?
items.correct: Curve C
items.misconception: Curve B
items.why: Students focus on the solution they are actively adding and describe the curve in terms of it, and textbooks show curves for both orders of addition. At zero volume added, the flask contains only the original solution, so the intercept is its pH. The curve then moves towards (but does not reach) the pH of the titrant.
items.specStatementText: pH curves for neutralization reactions involving strong acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.
items.random_wrong: Curve A

items.q: The graph shows the pH curve obtained when 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) is added to 25.0 cm³ of HCl(aq). What is the concentration of the HCl(aq)?
items.correct: 8.00 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³
items.misconception: 1.25 × 10⁻¹ mol dm⁻³
items.why:
Everyday reasoning links 'more' with 'stronger', and the inverse relationship between concentration and the volume needed for a fixed amount is counter-intuitive. c₁V₁ = c₂V₂ for a 1 : 1 reaction: a solution that needs twice the volume contains half the concentration. Find the amount of titrant at equivalence from its concentration and volume, then divide by the volume of the solution in the flask.

Working: The equivalence point is at the middle of the near-vertical section, at 20.0 cm³ of NaOH(aq). n(NaOH) = 0.100 mol dm⁻³ × 0.0200 dm³ = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O, so n(HCl) = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol. c(HCl) = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol / 0.0250 dm³ = 0.0800 mol dm⁻³. Check: the intercept, pH 1.1, gives [H⁺] = 10⁻¹·¹ = 0.08 mol dm⁻³, consistent with a fully ionized 0.0800 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq).
items.specStatementText: pH curves for neutralization reactions involving strong acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.
items.random_wrong: 1.00 × 10⁻¹ mol dm⁻³

items.q: The graph shows the pH curve for the titration of 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ of a weak monoprotic acid, HA, with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) at 298 K. Three points on the curve are labelled with their pH. What is the Ka of HA?
items.why:
The rule 'pH = pKa at half-equivalence' is memorized without its condition, and pKa is the one number given for the acid. From Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA], [H⁺] = Ka only when [A⁻]/[HA] = 1. A 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid solution has pH 2.88, not 4.76, and a buffer with twice as much acid as salt has pH 4.46.

Working: Equivalence is at 20.0 cm³ (steep section). At half-equivalence, 10.0 cm³, half the HA has been converted to A⁻, so [HA] = [A⁻] and Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA] = [H⁺]; hence pH = pKa. The curve gives pH 4.8 at 10.0 cm³, so pKa = 4.8 and Ka = 10⁻⁴·⁸ = 1.6 × 10⁻⁵.
items.specStatementText: pH curves of different combinations of strong and weak monoprotic acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.

items.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ of a weak acid, HA (pKa = 4.8), is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) at 298 K. The graph shows the pH curve, with the colour-change range of methyl red shaded. Which statement about using methyl red as the indicator for this titration is correct?
items.correct: It is unsuitable, as it changes colour gradually in the buffer region, before the equivalence point.
items.misconception: It is unsuitable, as its range does not include pH 7, the pH at the equivalence point.
items.why: The strong acid–strong base titration, whose salt (NaCl) is neutral, is the first and most familiar case, and the word 'neutralization' suggests a neutral product. Ions of the salt can react with water. CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻ makes sodium ethanoate basic, so the equivalence point of ethanoic acid with NaOH is about pH 8.7; NH₄⁺ makes ammonium chloride acidic.
items.specStatementText: An appropriate indicator for a titration has an end point range that coincides with the pH at the equivalence point.
items.random_wrong: It is suitable, as its range includes the pKa of HA, where the indicator should change.

items.q: The graph shows the pH curve for 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NH₃(aq) titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) at 298 K. pKa(NH₄⁺) = 9.25. The four bars beside the curve show the colour-change ranges of four indicators, 1 to 4, on the same pH scale. Which indicator is suitable for this titration?
items.correct: Indicator 2
items.misconception: Indicator 1
items.why:
'End' suggests the end of the curve or the end of the reaction, and the flat region after the steep section looks like the finish. The reaction is complete at the equivalence point in the middle of the steep section. The flat region beyond it is excess titrant; an indicator changing colour there would give too large a titre.

Working: Equivalence is at 25.0 cm³ (n(HCl) = n(NH₃) = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol). The flask then contains NH₄Cl(aq), [NH₄⁺] = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol / 0.0500 dm³ = 0.0500 mol dm⁻³; Ka(NH₄⁺) = 10⁻⁹·²⁵ = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰, so [H⁺] = √(5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 0.0500) = 5.3 × 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³ and pH ≈ 5.3, read from the middle of the steep section. The steep section spans roughly pH 3.5–7. Only bar 2 (4.4–6.2) lies within it and includes 5.3.
items.specStatementText: An appropriate indicator for a titration has an end point range that coincides with the pH at the equivalence point.

items.correct: Buffer P
items.misconception: Buffer Q
items.why: For a solution of an acid alone, more acid does mean a lower pH, and students carry this over without noticing that in a buffer the conjugate base concentration appears in the same expression. Compare the ratio [HA]/[A⁻] in each buffer: the larger the ratio, the larger [H⁺] and the lower the pH. Two buffers with the same ratio have the same pH whatever their absolute concentrations.

items.q: At 298 K, 0.10 mol dm⁻³ aqueous solutions have these pH values: HCl 1.0; CH₃COOH 2.9; NH₃ 11.1; NaOH 13.0. Which conclusion is supported by these data?
items.correct: CH₃COOH is a weak acid, as its [H⁺] is far below 0.10 mol dm⁻³.
items.misconception: HCl is only partly ionized in solution, as its pH is 1.0 rather than 0.0.
items.why:
Students meet equilibrium arrows for weak acids and assume every acid ionization is an equilibrium with the reactant side dominant; formula labels such as 'HNO₃(aq)' on bottles look like molecules. Strong acids ionize completely: HNO₃(aq) → H⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq), written with a single arrow. That complete ionization is what 'strong' means, and it is why [H⁺] equals the concentration of a strong monoprotic acid.

Working: HCl: pH 1.0 gives [H⁺] = 10⁻¹·⁰ = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, equal to the acid concentration (complete ionization). CH₃COOH: pH 2.9 gives [H⁺] = 10⁻²·⁹ = 1.3 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, about 1% of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ (partial ionization). NaOH: pH 13.0 gives [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹³, so [OH⁻] = Kw/[H⁺] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³ (complete). NH₃: pH 11.1 gives [H⁺] = 7.9 × 10⁻¹², [OH⁻] = 1.3 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, about 1% of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ (partial).
items.specStatementText: Strong and weak acids and bases differ in the extent of ionization.
items.random_wrong: NH₃ is a strong base, as its solution has a pH well above 7, at 11.1.

NH₃: pH 11.1 gives [H⁺] = 7.9 × 10⁻¹², [OH⁻] = 1.3 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, about 1% of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ (partial).

items.q: Can a substance act as a base only while it is dissolved in water?
items.correct: No. The Brønsted–Lowry definition concerns proton transfer, which can occur between an insoluble solid and an acid, or between gases such as NH₃(g) and HCl(g).
items.misconception: Acid–base behaviour happens only in aqueous solution, so a substance that does not dissolve in water cannot be a base.
items.why: Acids and bases are almost always met as aqueous solutions, and pH, indicators and neutralization are introduced in water, so 'in solution' becomes part of the concept. A base is defined by proton acceptance. Solid copper(II) oxide accepts protons from an acid; ammonia gas accepts protons from hydrogen chloride gas to form solid NH₄Cl. Being insoluble means CuO is not an alkali; it is still a base.
items.specStatementText: Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton donor and a Brønsted–Lowry base is a proton acceptor.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are the acid and base that react with each other a conjugate pair?
items.correct: No. The acid and base that react are on the same side of the equation; each one's conjugate is on the other side.
items.misconception: A conjugate acid–base pair is the acid and the base that react together, such as HNO₃ and NH₃.
items.why: 'Conjugate' is an unfamiliar word that suggests 'joined together', and acid–base reactions are first met as an acid reacting with a base. Each member of a conjugate pair is converted into the other by gain or loss of one proton. HNO₃ and NH₃ react together, but their formulae are unrelated; the pairs are HNO₃/NO₃⁻ and NH₄⁺/NH₃.
items.specStatementText: A pair of species differing by a single proton is called a conjugate acid–base pair.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can water act as a Brønsted–Lowry acid or base?
items.correct: Yes. Water is amphiprotic: it accepts H⁺ from HCl (base) and donates H⁺ to NH₃ (acid).
items.misconception: Water is neutral, so it cannot act as an acid or a base; it is only the solvent in which acid–base reactions happen.
items.why: Water is introduced as the neutral reference point (pH 7) and as the solvent, and it rarely appears in equations until Brønsted–Lowry theory. 'Neutral' describes pure water's [H⁺] = [OH⁻], not an inability to transfer protons. In NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ water donates H⁺; in HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻ it accepts H⁺.
items.specStatementText: Some species can act as both Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases.

items.q: Does an amphiprotic species act as an acid and a base in the same reaction?
items.correct: No. It can act as either, but in any one reaction it acts as one or the other, depending on its reaction partner.
items.misconception: An amphiprotic species acts as both an acid and a base at once in every reaction it takes part in.
items.why: The definition 'can act as both' is read as 'acts as both', and water's self-ionization (2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻, where one molecule of water is the acid and another the base) seems to confirm it. Amphiprotic describes an ability, not a role. With a stronger base such as NH₃, H₂PO₄⁻ donates H⁺; with a stronger acid such as H₃O⁺ it accepts H⁺. Its role is read from what happens to it in the equation.
items.specStatementText: Some species can act as both Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What quantity goes into pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]?
items.correct: The concentration of H⁺ in mol dm⁻³, found by converting any volume in cm³ to dm³ (÷ 1000) and dividing an amount by the solution's volume.
items.misconception: Any number produced on the way can be put into −log₁₀[H⁺]: a volume in cm³ can be used as if it were in dm³, or an amount in mol used as if it were a concentration.
items.why: Titration and dilution calculations mix cm³, dm³, mol and mol dm⁻³, and students under time pressure stop tracking units once a 'number for [H⁺]' appears. [H⁺] must be in mol dm⁻³. Convert cm³ to dm³ before multiplying by a concentration, and divide an amount in mol by the total volume in dm³ to get a concentration.
items.specStatementText: The pH scale can be used to describe the [H⁺] of a solution: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]; [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a pH meter give an accurate reading straight out of the box?
items.correct: No. A pH meter (probe) must first be calibrated with buffer solutions of known pH; only then are its readings accurate.
items.misconception: An electronic pH meter is automatically accurate and does not need calibration, because it is an instrument rather than a colour judgement.
items.why: Digital displays look authoritative, and in school practicals the calibration is often done by a technician before the lesson, so students never see it. The probe's response drifts with age, temperature and use. Calibrating against two or more buffers of known pH is what makes a pH meter both precise and accurate.
items.specStatementText: The pH scale can be used to describe the [H⁺] of a solution: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]; [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If an acid is added to water, does [OH⁻] change?
items.correct: Yes. [OH⁻] = Kw/[H⁺], so when [H⁺] rises, [OH⁻] falls in inverse proportion: a hundredfold rise in [H⁺] gives a hundredfold fall in [OH⁻].
items.misconception: [H⁺] and [OH⁻] are independent of each other, so each is judged on its own against its value in pure water at 298 K (1.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³): adding an acid increases [H⁺] but leaves [OH⁻] at its pure-water value.
items.why: Acids are associated with H⁺ and bases with OH⁻, so students picture two separate stores of ions and do not connect them through the water equilibrium. Both ions take part in one equilibrium, H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻, whose Kw is constant at a given temperature. Raising [H⁺] shifts the equilibrium left and removes OH⁻, so [OH⁻] = Kw/[H⁺].
items.specStatementText: The ion product constant of water, Kw, shows an inverse relationship between [H⁺] and [OH⁻]. Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻]
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a solution that contains H⁺(aq) ions have to be acidic?
items.correct: No. Every aqueous solution contains both H⁺ and OH⁻. It is acidic only if [H⁺] > [OH⁻].
items.misconception: Acidic solutions contain H⁺ ions and basic solutions contain OH⁻ ions, so a solution containing H⁺ ions is acidic.
items.why: Acids are introduced as 'substances that release H⁺' and bases as 'substances that release OH⁻', which suggests each ion belongs only to one kind of solution. Water's ionization means both ions are always present. Classification depends on comparing their concentrations: a solution of NaOH still contains H⁺, but far less than OH⁻.
items.specStatementText: The ion product constant of water, Kw, shows an inverse relationship between [H⁺] and [OH⁻]. Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻]
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does adding water to an acid neutralize it?
items.correct: No. Dilution lowers [H⁺] and raises the pH, but the solution stays acidic ([H⁺] > [OH⁻]) however much water is added; the pH approaches 7 but does not pass it.
items.misconception: Water neutralizes acid: adding water to an acidic solution removes its acidity, so any diluted acidic solution becomes neutral, pH 7.
items.why: Both dilution and neutralization make an acid 'less acidic', and students see the pH rise in both cases, so the two processes are merged. Neutralization removes H⁺ by reaction with a base; dilution only spreads the same H⁺ through more water. A strong acid such as HCl diluted a thousandfold from pH 1.0 has pH 4.0, still acidic.
items.specStatementText: Strong and weak acids and bases differ in the extent of ionization.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does an acid–base equilibrium lie on the side of the stronger acid and base?
items.correct: No. It lies on the side of the weaker acid and the weaker base.
items.misconception: An acid–base equilibrium lies on the side of the stronger acid and base, because strong species are the ones that are favoured.
items.why: 'Strong' sounds like 'dominant' or 'favoured', and students imagine the strong species 'winning' and so being present in the larger amount. A strong acid donates its proton readily, so it is used up; a strong base accepts readily, so it is used up too. The species left in large amounts are those least inclined to react further: the weaker acid and weaker base.
items.specStatementText: Strong and weak acids and bases differ in the extent of ionization.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do acids react with bases and carbonates to produce hydrogen gas?
items.correct: No. Hydrogen is produced when an acid reacts with a reactive metal. Acid–base reactions transfer H⁺ to the base; carbonates give carbon dioxide, not hydrogen.
items.misconception: Acids release hydrogen gas in all their reactions, so the gas formed when an acid reacts with a carbonate is hydrogen (or includes hydrogen).
items.why: The acid + metal → salt + hydrogen reaction is learned early and is closely associated with 'the fizzing of acids', and acids are described as 'containing hydrogen'. In neutralization the H⁺ is accepted by the base: by OH⁻ or O²⁻ to give water, by CO₃²⁻ or HCO₃⁻ to give water and CO₂. H₂ forms only when a metal reduces H⁺.
items.specStatementText: Acids react with bases in neutralization reactions.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can weak acids such as ethanoic acid neutralize bases and react with carbonates?
items.correct: Yes. Weak acids undergo all the typical acid reactions; ethanoic acid reacts with sodium carbonate to give sodium ethanoate, water and carbon dioxide.
items.misconception: A weak acid is too weak to react with bases or carbonates; only strong acids take part in neutralization reactions.
items.why: 'Weak' is taken to mean 'unreactive', and vinegar is known as a harmless food ingredient rather than a laboratory acid. Weakness refers to the extent of ionization in water, not to whether the acid can react. As the base removes H⁺, more of the weak acid ionizes, so the reaction goes to completion; vinegar fizzing with baking soda is an everyday example.
items.specStatementText: Acids react with bases in neutralization reactions.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are a salt's parent acid and parent base the ions present in the salt?
items.correct: No. The parent acid and base are the neutral acid and base that reacted to form the salt: CH₃NH₃Cl comes from HCl and CH₃NH₂, not from Cl⁻ and CH₃NH₃⁺.
items.misconception: The parent acid and parent base of a salt are simply its anion and cation, so the parent base of CH₃NH₃Cl is CH₃NH₃⁺.
items.why: The salt's ions are the species visible in the formula, and students take 'parent' to mean 'the parts it is made of'. Work backwards through the proton transfer: remove the H⁺ that the base gained to find the parent base (CH₃NH₃⁺ − H⁺ = CH₃NH₂), and add H⁺ to the anion to find the parent acid (Cl⁻ + H⁺ = HCl).
items.specStatementText: Acids react with bases in neutralization reactions.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the pH rise by the same amount for each cm³ of alkali added in a titration?
items.correct: No. The pH changes only slowly at first, then very sharply around the equivalence point, then slowly again, because pH is logarithmic.
items.misconception: pH changes linearly with the volume of alkali added, so the pH curve is a straight line from the starting pH to the final pH.
items.why: Students extrapolate from quantities that change in proportion to the volume added (such as the amount of NaOH), and do not connect the logarithmic definition of pH to the shape of the curve. Until nearly all the acid is used up, each addition removes only a small fraction of the H⁺, so pH barely changes. Around equivalence, [H⁺] falls by many powers of ten for a fraction of a cm³, giving the near-vertical section.
items.specStatementText: pH curves for neutralization reactions involving strong acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In the weak acid approximation, is [H⁺] = Ka × [HA] or √(Ka × [HA])?
items.correct: [H⁺] = √(Ka × [HA]), because Ka ≈ [H⁺]²/[HA] when [H⁺] = [A⁻].
items.misconception: For a weak acid, [H⁺] = Ka × [HA]initial, with no square root.
items.why: Students remember that Ka and [HA] are multiplied but not that the product equals [H⁺]², because [H⁺] and [A⁻] are written as two separate terms in the Ka expression. Because each HA that ionizes gives one H⁺ and one A⁻, [H⁺] = [A⁻], so Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA] = [H⁺]²/[HA]. Rearranging gives [H⁺] = √(Ka × [HA]).
items.specStatementText: For a conjugate acid–base pair, the relationship Ka × Kb = Kw can be derived from the expressions for Ka and Kb.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the dissolving of a salt into its ions a hydrolysis reaction?
items.correct: No. Dissolving (NH₄Cl(s) → NH₄⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)) produces ions but does not change [H⁺]. Hydrolysis is the subsequent proton transfer between an ion and water.
items.misconception: The equation for a salt dissolving and separating into its ions is its hydrolysis equation, and it explains the pH of the solution.
items.why: Both processes happen when a salt is added to water and both involve water, so the dissociation equation is written as the 'reaction with water'. An equation explains a pH change only if it produces or consumes H⁺ (H₃O⁺) or OH⁻. The dissociation equation does neither; the hydrolysis equation NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺ does.
items.specStatementText: The pH of a salt solution depends on the relative strengths of the parent acid and base.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: At equilibrium, are the reactants and products present in equal amounts?
items.correct: No. At equilibrium the rates of the forward and backward reactions are equal; the concentrations are constant but usually not equal.
items.misconception: At equilibrium the two sides are present in equal amounts, so an indicator at equilibrium always contains equal amounts of HInd and Ind⁻.
items.why: The word 'equilibrium' suggests balance or equality, and diagrams often show the two sides of a balance level. Equal rates, not equal concentrations, define equilibrium. For an indicator, [Ind⁻]/[HInd] = Ka/[H⁺], so the ratio depends on pH: equal amounts only when pH = pKa.
items.specStatementText: Acid–base indicators are weak acids, where the components of the conjugate acid–base pair have different colours. The pH of the end point of an indicator, where it changes colour, approximately corresponds to its pKa value.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is HInd or Ind⁻ the main form of an indicator when the pH is above its pKa?
items.correct: Ind⁻. When pH > pKa, [H⁺] < Ka, so [Ind⁻]/[HInd] = Ka/[H⁺] > 1.
items.misconception: When the pH is above the pKa, the undissociated form HInd predominates.
items.why: Two inverted scales are involved (a higher pH means a lower [H⁺]; a larger pKa means a smaller Ka), and students invert one of them. Removing H⁺ (raising the pH) shifts HInd ⇌ H⁺ + Ind⁻ to the right. So above the pKa, Ind⁻ predominates and the solution shows the colour of Ind⁻.
items.specStatementText: Acid–base indicators are weak acids, where the components of the conjugate acid–base pair have different colours. The pH of the end point of an indicator, where it changes colour, approximately corresponds to its pKa value.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is an indicator's colour change a neutralization that forms a coloured salt?
items.correct: No. The colour change is a shift in the equilibrium HInd ⇌ H⁺ + Ind⁻ between two differently coloured forms; the indicator is present in tiny amounts and does not neutralize the solution.
items.misconception: An indicator changes colour because it reacts with the acid or alkali to form a coloured salt.
items.why: Colour changes in chemistry are often taught as signs of a new substance forming, and acids and bases are known to form salts. The indicator's own acid–base equilibrium responds to [H⁺]. Adding acid shifts it towards HInd; adding alkali towards Ind⁻. The change is reversible and happens at a characteristic pH.
items.specStatementText: Acid–base indicators are weak acids, where the components of the conjugate acid–base pair have different colours. The pH of the end point of an indicator, where it changes colour, approximately corresponds to its pKa value.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a buffer a neutral solution?
items.correct: No. A buffer resists changes in pH at whatever pH it has; acidic buffers such as ethanoic acid/ethanoate have pH below 7 and basic buffers such as NH₃/NH₄⁺ have pH above 7.
items.misconception: A buffer is a neutral solution (pH 7), so a mixture of neutral salts such as NaCl and KNO₃ acts as a buffer.
items.why: Buffers are associated with keeping conditions 'normal' or 'balanced', and 'neutral' seems the natural balanced state. Buffering depends on having both a weak acid and its conjugate base. A solution of neutral salts has neither, so a small addition of acid or alkali changes its pH greatly.
items.specStatementText: A buffer solution is one that resists change in pH on the addition of small amounts of acid or alkali.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do the spectator ions of a buffer take part in buffering?
items.correct: No. Ions such as Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectators; buffering is done by the conjugate acid–base pair.
items.misconception: The spectator ions do the buffering: for example, Na⁺ from sodium ethanoate combines with Cl⁻ from added HCl to form NaCl and so removes the added acid.
items.why: Buffers are described as containing 'a salt', and students imagine the salt's ions reacting to form another salt. Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in water remain as separate hydrated ions; forming 'NaCl' in solution removes no H⁺ or OH⁻. It is proton transfer to or from the conjugate pair that keeps the pH nearly constant.
items.specStatementText: A buffer solution is one that resists change in pH on the addition of small amounts of acid or alkali.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a buffer keep the pH exactly constant?
items.correct: No. A buffer keeps the pH nearly constant. The ratio of its components changes slightly on each addition, so the pH changes slightly.
items.misconception: A buffer keeps the pH exactly constant when acid or alkali is added.
items.why: 'Resists change' is read as 'prevents change', and textbook demonstrations show the pH meter hardly moving. Adding H⁺ to a CH₃COOH/CH₃COO⁻ buffer converts some CH₃COO⁻ into CH₃COOH, so the ratio [CH₃COOH]/[CH₃COO⁻] rises a little and the pH falls a little. Large additions exhaust the buffer entirely.
items.specStatementText: A buffer solution is one that resists change in pH on the addition of small amounts of acid or alkali.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does diluting a buffer lower its pH because the weak acid ionizes to a greater extent?
items.correct: No. The fraction of acid ionized rises slightly on dilution, but the H⁺ is spread through a larger volume; in a buffer the pH is set by Ka and the ratio [HA]/[A⁻], which dilution does not change.
items.misconception: Dilution makes a weak acid ionize to a greater extent, so a diluted buffer contains a higher [H⁺] and has a lower pH.
items.why: Students learn that the degree of ionization of a weak acid increases on dilution and confuse a larger fraction ionized with a larger concentration of H⁺. A larger fraction ionized does not mean a larger [H⁺]: dilution lowers [H⁺] for a weak acid alone. In a buffer the large amount of A⁻ already present suppresses ionization, and [H⁺] = Ka[HA]/[A⁻] stays essentially the same.
items.specStatementText: The pH of a buffer solution depends on both: the pKa or pKb of its acid or base; the ratio of the concentration of acid or base to the concentration of the conjugate base or acid.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a salt whose anion still contains an ionizable H, such as NaHCO₃, always give an acidic solution?
items.correct: No. An anion such as HCO₃⁻ is amphiprotic: it can donate H⁺ (governed by its Ka) or accept H⁺ (governed by its Kb). The solution is basic if the ion's Kb exceeds its Ka, as for HCO₃⁻ (pKb 7.65 < pKa 10.33), and acidic if Ka exceeds Kb, as for HSO₄⁻.
items.misconception: A salt whose anion still contains a hydrogen that can be donated (an 'acid salt' such as NaHCO₃) gives an acidic solution, because that hydrogen is released as H⁺.
items.why: Salts such as NaHCO₃ and NaHSO₄ are traditionally called 'acid salts', 'hydrogen' appears in their names, and students consider only the ion's reaction as an acid, not its competing reaction as a base. Compare the anion's Ka with its Kb (Kb = Kw / Ka of its conjugate acid). For HCO₃⁻, Kb = 10⁻⁷·⁶⁵ is larger than Ka = 10⁻¹⁰·³³, so HCO₃⁻ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ + OH⁻ dominates and NaHCO₃(aq) is weakly basic.
items.specStatementText: The pH of a salt solution depends on the relative strengths of the parent acid and base.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a mixture of NH₃ and NH₄Cl an acidic buffer, since NH₄Cl is an acidic salt?
items.correct: No. The type of buffer is set by its weak parent, not by the salt. NH₃ with NH₄⁺ is a basic buffer: with 0.20 mol NH₃ and 0.10 mol NH₄⁺ in 1.00 dm³, pH = pKa(NH₄⁺) + log₁₀(0.20/0.10) = 9.25 + 0.30 = 9.55. CH₃COOH with CH₃COO⁻ is an acidic buffer (pH 4.76 for equal amounts), although CH₃COONa is a basic salt.
items.misconception: A buffer takes the character of the salt it contains: a buffer containing an acidic salt such as NH₄Cl is an acidic buffer, and one containing a basic salt such as CH₃COONa is a basic buffer.
items.why: Salt hydrolysis teaches NH₄Cl(aq) as acidic and CH₃COONa(aq) as basic, and buffers are introduced as 'a weak acid or weak base with its salt', so students classify the buffer by its salt. Classify a buffer by its weak parent: a weak acid with a salt of that acid (CH₃COOH/CH₃COO⁻) is an acidic buffer; a weak base with a salt of that base (NH₃/NH₄⁺) is a basic buffer.
items.specStatementText: A buffer solution is one that resists change in pH on the addition of small amounts of acid or alkali.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does titrating a weak acid always give an equivalence point above pH 7?
items.correct: No. The equivalence pH depends on the salt formed, so on both the acid and the base. For CH₃COOH titrated with NH₃, the salt contains CH₃COO⁻ and NH₄⁺, which hydrolyse to similar extents (pKa of CH₃COOH 4.76, pKb of NH₃ 4.75), so the equivalence pH is about 7.
items.misconception: The equivalence pH is fixed by the substance being titrated alone: a weak acid gives an equivalence point above pH 7 whatever base is added.
items.why: The rule 'weak acid–strong base: equivalence above 7' is memorised as 'weak acid: above 7', dropping the condition on the base. Identify the salt at equivalence and consider both of its ions. With a strong base only the weak acid's conjugate base hydrolyses, so the pH is above 7; when both partners are weak, the two ions compete and the pH depends on their relative strengths.
items.specStatementText: pH curves of different combinations of strong and weak monoprotic acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In H₂CO₃(aq) ⇌ HCO₃⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq), is HCO₃⁻ acting as a base in the forward reaction?
items.correct: No. In the forward reaction HCO₃⁻ is formed when H₂CO₃ donates a proton; it is the conjugate base of H₂CO₃. HCO₃⁻ acts as a base only in a reaction in which it accepts a proton, such as HCO₃⁻ + H₃O⁺ ⇌ H₂CO₃ + H₂O.
items.misconception: A species labelled 'conjugate base' in an equation is acting as a base in that reaction, so an equation that forms HCO₃⁻ from H₂CO₃ shows HCO₃⁻ behaving as a base.
items.why: Equations are annotated with 'acid, base, conjugate acid, conjugate base' across both sides, and students take the label 'conjugate base' to mean that the species is doing what a base does in the reaction shown. Decide the role from the forward reaction: the reactant that gains H⁺ is acting as the base. A product labelled 'conjugate base' acts as a base only in the reverse reaction.
items.specStatementText: Some species can act as both Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the pH of aqueous sodium ethanoate set by the ionization of ethanoic acid?
items.correct: No. The salt supplies CH₃COO⁻ and Na⁺ ions, not CH₃COOH molecules. The CH₃COO⁻ ion accepts H⁺ from water, CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻, so CH₃COONa(aq) is basic.
items.misconception: A salt behaves in water like its parent acid, so the ionization of that acid (CH₃COOH + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H₃O⁺) explains the pH of its salt, and sodium ethanoate solution is acidic.
items.why: The salt is named after its parent acid (ethanoate from ethanoic acid), and the ionization equation of ethanoic acid is the one students have written most often; predicting a salt's pH from the acid in its name is commonly reported in teaching of salt hydrolysis. Write the ions actually present in the salt and ask which one reacts with water: the conjugate base of a weak acid accepts H⁺ and releases OH⁻.
items.specStatementText: The pH of a salt solution depends on the relative strengths of the parent acid and base.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does 'equivalence point' mean the point at which equal volumes or equal concentrations of acid and base have been mixed?
items.correct: No. It is the point at which the amounts (in mol) are in the ratio of the equation. The volumes and concentrations are equal only in the special case where the two solutions happen to have the same concentration.
items.misconception: At the equivalence point equal volumes of acid and base have been mixed, so the two solutions have the same concentration.
items.why: 'Equivalence' is heard as 'equal', and the introductory example (25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ acid needing 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ base) has equal volumes and equal concentrations. Equivalence means stoichiometrically equivalent amounts: n(acid) = n(base) for a monoprotic acid and a base with one OH⁻. Read the equivalence volume from the steep section of the curve and use n = cV to find the unknown concentration.
items.specStatementText: pH curves for neutralization reactions involving strong acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the equivalence point where the pH curve levels off after the steep section?
items.correct: No. The equivalence point is at the middle of the steep, near-vertical section. The flat region beyond it is excess titrant.
items.misconception: The equivalence point is where the pH curve levels off after the steep section, because that is where the pH stops changing and the reaction is complete.
items.why: The flat region looks like the 'finish' of the curve, and 'the reaction is complete' is heard as 'nothing more changes'. The reaction is complete at the middle of the steep section; the pH there jumps because a single drop switches the flask from slight excess acid to slight excess base. Beyond it the flat region is simply the pH of the excess titrant.
items.specStatementText: pH curves for neutralization reactions involving strong acids and bases have characteristic shapes and features.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the concentration of the acid found by dividing its amount by the total volume at the equivalence point?
items.correct: No. The amount of acid was originally contained in the 25.0 cm³ placed in the flask, so its concentration is n/0.0250 dm³; the total volume (acid + base added) is used only for the concentration of species in the mixture after mixing.
items.misconception: The original concentration of the acid is its amount divided by the total volume of the mixture at the equivalence point (volume of acid + volume of alkali added).
items.why: Students calculate concentrations of excess reagent or salt in the flask by dividing by the total volume, and carry that step over to finding the concentration of the original solution. Divide the amount of acid by the volume of acid solution used (25.0 cm³), not by the mixed volume.
